title: She Looked Pure on the Outside… But No One Knew the War in Her Mind
paragraphs:
She Looked Pure on the Outside… But No One Knew the War in Her Mind
Why Women Also Battle Lust—and the Grace That Still Finds Them There
She sat in the front row.

Bible open. Notes written neatly. Worship hands raised at the right moments. She knew the lyrics, the language, the posture. If you passed her in church, you would have called her “strong,” “disciplined,” maybe even “set apart.”
But you would have been wrong about one thing.
You would have never guessed the war she fought when no one was looking.
Because somewhere between the sermons and the silence… her mind betrayed her.
And she hated herself for it.

No one told her that women could struggle with lust too. No one said it out loud. The silence in the church felt louder than her thoughts. Lust was always preached as a man’s battle, a male weakness, a male sin. So when it showed up in her life, she didn’t just feel temptation…
She felt like a contradiction.
Like something was deeply wrong with her.
So she buried it.
But what is buried doesn’t die. It grows roots.
Jesus didn’t stay silent about this kind of struggle.
He said in Matthew 5:28:
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

In the original Greek, the phrase “lustful intent” is πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn), rooted in ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō)—which means not just physical desire, but a deep, consuming craving of the heart.
This was never just a male issue.
This was always a human issue.
Because lust doesn’t live in the body first.
It lives in the heart.
And Scripture is painfully honest about the human heart.
In Jeremiah 17:9, written in Hebrew:

“עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא” (ʿāqōb ha-lēḇ mikkōl wəʾānūš hūʾ)
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick…”
Not male heart.
Not female heart.
Human heart.
And hers was tired of pretending.

She tried to fight it quietly. She made promises to God she couldn’t keep. She deleted things, avoided places, prayed desperate prayers at night only to fall again the next day. The cycle became exhausting. The shame became heavier than the sin itself.
And then came the lie that almost destroyed her:
“Good Christian women don’t struggle with this.”
But the truth?
Holiness isn’t pretending you’re not in a battle.
Holiness is bringing your real battle into the light.
Because darkness only survives where there is secrecy.
And she had been hiding too long.
James 1:14–15 says:
“But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire.”

The Greek word for “desire” here is again ἐπιθυμία (epithymia)—the same root. Lust is not foreign to us. It is familiar. It whispers in our language. It knows our weaknesses. It studies our loneliness.
And for her, it didn’t always look obvious.
Sometimes it was emotional dependency.
Sometimes it was fantasy.
Sometimes it was longing for validation that slowly turned into something deeper, something more consuming.
Lust isn’t always loud.
Sometimes it’s quiet… and that’s what makes it dangerous.
But here’s where the story shifts.
Because Jesus never exposed sin just to condemn it.
He exposed it to redeem it.
In John 8, a woman caught in sexual sin was thrown before Him. Public shame. Public accusation. Public humiliation. The kind of moment that destroys a person’s identity forever.
But Jesus bends down.
Writes in the dust.
And then says:
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
In Greek: οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω (oude egō se katakrinō) — “Neither do I condemn you.”
Notice that.
He didn’t deny her sin.
He denied her condemnation.
That means your struggle does not disqualify you from His mercy.
Even the one thing you’re most ashamed of.
Even the thoughts you’ve never told anyone.
Even the cycles you thought you’d never break.
Especially those.
This is where grace begins to rewrite the story.
Not by ignoring sin.
But by meeting you in it and refusing to leave you there.
Romans 5:8 reminds us:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
While.
Not after you fixed it.
Not after you became “pure enough.”
While you were still in the middle of it.
That includes her.
That includes you.
So if you’ve been silently fighting this… you’re not alone.
And you’re not beyond restoration.
You’re being invited into honesty.
Into healing.
Into freedom that doesn’t come from pretending—but from surrender.
Be honest.
Did this hit somewhere you’ve been hiding?
Let this be the moment you stop pretending.
If you’re serious about going deeper—about real healing, real discipleship, real transformation—we’ve built something for you.
If you want to grow… if you want accountability… if you want to walk this out for real…
Because supporting truth is part of glorifying God too.
You don’t just consume light.
You help spread it.
And someone else’s freedom might begin with what you choose to share.

Because the war you’re fighting in silence…
Jesus is ready to heal in the open.
